answer.rationale: Finance mandate of -18% component spend is binding, and the incumbent contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew. memory_c2 (already verified directionally) shows the low-cost vendor delivered a sharp unit-cost cut with fast onboarding and accurate invoicing on the prior move — that is the only inherited evidence pointing at a vendor capable of meeting the mandate alone. memory_c3 shows adding a second source mitigated a single point of failure during a shortage; I am pulling it because the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, meaning delivery risk is elevated and a sole-source switch would expose that. The single decision this cycle must minimize TCO without raising delivery risk. The low-cost vendor's quote meets the mandate alone, so switching primary captures the full cost reduction now. To keep delivery risk from rising on a 94%-utilization line with no buffer, I would pair the switch with a small, time-bounded dual-source overlap — effectively a guarded test of the new primary while the incumbent remains available as a second source for the transition window. That preserves the buffer without spending the second decision slot, and keeps a fallback if the new primary falters at volume. I am not choosing add_second_source as the standalone action because it does not by itself hit the -18% mandate. I am not choosing renew_incumbent or negotiate_terms because neither is likely to close an 18% gap in 14 days, and the incumbent's contract does not auto-renew, so deferral would push us past expiry. I am not choosing defer_decision for the same reason — expiry makes deferral equivalent to a forced scramble. Two uncertainties remain and should be carried into execution rather than papered over: (1) the low-cost vendor's prior accuracy record (memory_c2) is from a different component context and may not transfer perfectly to higher-volume line conditions; (2) the dual-source overlap adds administrative and minimum-order cost that could partially erode the headline unit-cost saving, so the net TCO win needs confirmation against actual volumes once the first billing cycle lands. If the archived sources materially contradict this read, I will revisit.
